## **Supply improves, demand growth slows – all change for the copper balance** 







#### In a nutshell 

- We have reduced our **demand** forecast globally from 3.5% to 2.5% in 2012 mainly due to China’s slowdown and Europe’s ongoing woes 

- 2013 has also been pulled back as some regions still finding the bottom 

### ...meanwhile.... 

- .... **supply** has performed better than expected, with limited disruptions 

- compared to recent years, allowing us to increase 2012 forecast growth to 2.0%. We continue to expect strong growth in mine supply in 2013 

- As a result.... 

- ...CRU’s global refined copper supply/demand **balance*** has moved to a minor surplus for 2012, which is set to expand in 2013 to over 180,000t. 

- After all stock changes, inc. Shanghai bonded warehouse stocks 

#### **Demand seen lower but finding the bottom** 

- 2012 - Slight downturn in refined consumption growth due to: 

   - Euro debt crisis, working stocks of refined copper reduced to bare minimum, minimal buying activity, 

   - China’s continuing tight credit, lacklustre power investment, domestic appliance industry shocked by weak exports and high stock levels, stimulus package too late to have significant impact on full year refined consumption 

   - North American refined consumption saw strong growth despite political turmoil, driven by strong growth in the automotive industry 

##### • Quarter ahead: 

- Promise of late China recovery in copper demand now very unlikely as Northern China’s cold winter reduces construction activity.  Back-weighted power distribution investment should support refined consumption level in Q4. 

- Seasonal downturns expected in Europe and North America as end-of-year stock liquidation takes place.  North American copper demand expected to have another strong quarter due to auto production forecasts. 

##### •

##### Next year: - Unspent & rolled-over investment in China expected to support refined demand. Particularly power and rail. - Chinese home appliance stimulus and uptick in European economies to result in more promising refined copper demand from China’s domestic appliance manufacturers in 2013. - Rest of Asia anticipated to see more organic growth following effects of earthquake/tsunami/meltdown in Japan, flooding in Thailand, and turbulence in China’s economic growth settle. - Potential of demand pick-up in Europe closely related to political events regarding macroeconomy. Currently, stilted y- o-y IP growth expected. - North American refined copper demand expected to turn flat to negative due to startup of new scrap-fed wirerod mill. Data: LMCA , CRU, INEGI #### **Supply has confounded expectations** - 2012 has seen far fewer disruptions to mine supply than anticipated. - So far just 32 days of production have been lost due to strikes compared to 116

in the same period of 2011. - Ore grades have reversed their decline. - A 2.4% rise in mine output is now forecast for 2012. - This improved performance is expected to be maintained into 2013. ### **But risks remain going forwards** - Labour contracts at major South American mines are due for renewal in Q4 2012 and Q1 2013, with potential for strike losses. - Mine projects are at risk of delay and cancellation in the current uncertain economic and financial climate. #### **Losses & gains balanced, allowing mine supply to increase...** Y-o-y change at major producers*, ‘000t contained Cu, H1 2011 – H1 2012

#### **Higher supply and lower consumption has switched our 2012 balance to surplus** - Our raw refined supply/demand balance indicates a surplus of 211,000t for 2012... - ...but accounting for high stocking in Shanghai’s bonded warehouses in 2012 takes this to a surplus of just 11,000t. - Shanghai bonded stocks have risen again to reach 650,000-700,00t in the last two weeks, indicating weak sentiments in China

for Q4 - The LME copper price is currently above $8,000/t, having primarily followed US dollar moves this year, but weaker China and Europe lead us to forecast prices moving lower in Q4 and Q1. - However, stimulus packages from the Chinese government should impact physical demand by Q2, supporting prices mid-year, before the wave of new supply towards the end of the year drives a large surplus and corresponding fall in prices.
